summary: Describes the Mailbox Update (MUPDATE) protocol, which lets a group of IMAP or POP servers share a distributed mailbox database. This allows many machines to share the work of mail delivery instead of depending on a single machine. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: One mail room can get overloaded or break. This lets many mail rooms share one up-to-date list of who lives where, so mail still gets delivered if one room stops.

questions: how does mupdate reserve a mailbox
what is the difference between a mupdate master and slave
subtitle: A small text protocol that lets many mail servers share one authoritative list of which mailbox lives where.

tldr.problem: A single machine handling mail delivery is limited in capacity, and its failure stops delivery for every user. Spreading mailboxes over many IMAP or POP3 servers needs them to agree, atomically, on one mailbox namespace.
tldr.mechanism: One master server keeps the authoritative mailbox database. Slave servers and other clients connect to it over TCP, and a slave issues UPDATE to receive a stream of every change. New mailboxes are claimed with RESERVE and then made live with ACTIVATE.
tldr.outcome: MUPDATE is an Experimental protocol, not an Internet standard. It trusts every authenticated user completely, and it is updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 3656 is an Experimental protocol specification, not an Internet standard, and it is updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Why a Shared Mailbox Database
sections.content:
As demand for high-performance mail delivery grows, the RFC argues that single-machine solutions are inadequate. They hit capacity limits, and if the one machine fails, mail delivery stops for all users. It is preferable to let many machines share the work.

The Mailbox Update (MUPDATE) protocol lets a group of IMAP or POP3 servers act with a unified mailbox namespace. To do that, the servers need atomic mailbox operations and enough guarantees about database consistency. The primary goal of the protocol is to be simple to implement while still giving consistency between participants.
sections.eli5: If one mail room breaks, nobody gets mail. With many mail rooms sharing one list of who lives where, the others can keep working.

sections.title: Master, Slaves and Clients
sections.content:
MUPDATE assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP, and IANA has registered port 3905 with the short name mupdate. There are three kinds of participants: a single master server, slave (replica) servers, and clients. The master holds the authoritative copy of the mailbox database.

Slaves connect to the master as ordinary clients and act as replicas. End clients may connect to the master or to any slave and search the database. Operations that change the database can only be performed against the master.

Every command carries a unique alphanumeric tag. Commands MAY be pipelined, but the server MUST execute them in the order received. If a server has an inactivity timeout, it MUST be at least 15 minutes.
sections.eli5: One mail room keeps the real list and is the only one allowed to change it. The other rooms keep copies and can answer questions about it.

sections.title: Atoms, Strings and Responses
sections.content:
Data uses formats similar to ACAP: atoms and strings. Commands and tags are atoms, which are alphanumeric and MUST be less than 15 octets long. Everything else is a string, either quoted or a literal given as an octet count in braces. Both sides MUST support lines of at least 1024 octets, and servers MUST support literals of at least 4096 octets.

Each tagged response starts with the tag of the command it answers. OK means success, NO means the request was denied or failed, BAD means the command could not be understood, and BYE means the server is closing the connection. Each of these carries a human-readable string.

Two responses describe database records. RESERVE carries a mailbox name and a location string, and says the name is no longer available in the namespace without saying the mailbox is ready. MAILBOX carries the name, a location and an IMAP ACL string, and says the mailbox is ready for clients. A DELETE response, valid only during an update stream, tells a slave to remove a mailbox.
sections.eli5: Messages are short lines with a tag, like a ticket number, so you can match each answer to your question. Some answers say a name is held for someone, and others say the mailbox is ready to use.

sections.title: Commands and Mailbox Creation
sections.content:
The client commands are AUTHENTICATE, ACTIVATE, DEACTIVATE, DELETE, FIND, LIST, LOGOUT, NOOP, RESERVE, STARTTLS and UPDATE. Before a successful AUTHENTICATE, the server MUST NOT accept anything except AUTHENTICATE, STARTTLS and LOGOUT. AUTHENTICATE starts a SASL negotiation with the service name mupdate, and implementations are REQUIRED to implement the GSSAPI mechanism.

FIND returns the record for one mailbox, and LIST acts like FIND across the whole database, optionally filtered by a location prefix. The commands that change data, RESERVE, ACTIVATE, DEACTIVATE and DELETE, MUST NOT be issued to a slave.

Creating a mailbox is a two-step process. The client sends RESERVE with the name and location. If the server answers OK, the name is held; if NO, another server may already have reserved it. The client then does its local mailbox creation and sends ACTIVATE with the name, location and ACL. DEACTIVATE moves an active mailbox back to the reserved state.

A slave uses UPDATE to stay current. The server first returns every record, as LIST would, then an OK, and from then on the master MUST stream each change to the slave within 30 seconds. After UPDATE, the client may only send NOOP and LOGOUT. A slave can send NOOP and wait for the OK to know its copy is current as of that moment.
sections.eli5: To make a new mailbox you first put a sign saying 'this name is mine', then set it up, then announce it is ready. A copy-keeping room asks once for the whole list and after that gets a message for every change.

sections.title: TLS, SASL and Trust
sections.content:
Unauthenticated users cannot search or change the database. The server may support STARTTLS, which begins a TLS negotiation right after the OK response. After TLS is up, the server MUST send its capability banner again, which protects against a man-in-the-middle altering the list before STARTTLS. The client MUST discard its cached capabilities and use the new ones.

The RFC is frank about the limits. The specification assumes no protection of any kind for authenticated users: all of them have complete access to the database, so accounts using it must be well secured. A more secure deployment might send read-only access through slaves and keep write access to the master, at the cost of a marginally longer time for updates to reach clients.

The protocol also assumes authenticated users cooperate to keep operations atomic. New mailboxes SHOULD be RESERVEd before ACTIVATE, even though the protocol does not require it, so participants that ignore the locking could create an inconsistent database. The RFC also defines a mupdate:// URL scheme, with a server-only form and a form that names a mailbox to FIND.
sections.eli5: Once you are let in, you can change anything on the list, so the key to the door must be guarded. Everyone is also trusted to follow the rule of reserving a name before using it.
